There is a particular pleasure in not knowing something yet.

Not the feeling of being lost, but the moment just before understanding: when a question has become clear enough to follow, and the answer is still somewhere ahead.

## Follow a smaller question

Big questions are useful as directions. Small questions are useful as starting points.

Instead of “How does learning work?”, try “What do I remember from yesterday?” Instead of “How do I build something meaningful?”, try “What is one small thing I wish existed?”

The smaller question gives you something you can actually try.

## Make something you can move

An explanation becomes more memorable when you can change something and see what happens. A slider turns a formula into a conversation.

Consider a simple wave:

$$
y(t) = A\sin(\omega t)
$$

The amplitude $A$ changes its height. The angular frequency $\omega$ changes how quickly it repeats. You can read those words, or you can try it in [the wave playground](/blog/component-showcase/#a-sine-wave).

## Keep a trail

A note doesn't have to be a conclusion. It can be a question, a sketch, a failed experiment, or a sentence you want to return to.

- Write the question down.
- Try the smallest useful experiment.
- Notice what surprised you.
- Leave a note for your future self.

Over time, a collection of small questions becomes a map of what you care about.

_This is a demonstration essay, ready to replace with your own._
